caption:
A faceless AI video pipeline in 7 free steps.

No camera. No studio. Just a stack you can copy:

→ Script: free models through one endpoint (FreeLLMAPI or OmniRoute)
→ Voice: Kokoro-82M, an open-weight voice model with Apache-licensed weights
→ B-roll: screen-record the real page with OBS Studio
→ Motion: Remotion, free for individuals and companies of up to 3 people
→ Sound: Freesound, filtered to CC0
→ Captions: transcribe your own voiceover, then fix names by hand
→ Schedule: Buffer's free plan, 3 channels

The step people skip is B-roll. A real screen recording of the actual repo or docs page is far more believable than a stock clip of someone typing.

The honest part: free tiers have caps, licences differ, and open models still make confident mistakes. Every fact still needs a human check.

I've put the prompts and the catch for each step in the carousel.

article:
## The pipeline in one line

Script → voice → B-roll → motion → sound → captions → schedule. Each step has a free option, and none of them needs your face on camera. Here is the stack I'd use, with the catch for each step.

## 01 · Script with free models

Write the script with an LLM routed through FreeLLMAPI or OmniRoute. Both are open-source projects that put many free tiers behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so a rate limit on one provider doesn't stop your run. A prompt to start with:

> Write a 70-word voiceover for a 35-second video. One idea per line. Plain British English. Every number needs a source link I can check.

Then read every claim yourself. Free models make confident mistakes.

## 02 · Voice with an open model

Kokoro-82M is an open-weight text-to-speech model with 82 million parameters and Apache-licensed weights. On Hugging Face's new Open TTS Leaderboard, published on 30 September, it's one of three models leading on English word error rate, alongside `Supertone/supertonic-3` and `fishaudio/s2-pro`. The leaderboard measures intelligibility, speed and speaker similarity, not how natural a voice sounds, so use its Listen tab before you pick. Write lines you can say in one breath.

## 03 · B-roll from real screens

Record the actual thing you're talking about: the GitHub repo, the docs page, the changelog. OBS Studio is free, open-source software for recording and streaming on Windows, Mac and Linux. A real screen is more believable than a stock clip of someone typing, and it shows you did the homework.

## 04 · Motion graphics in code

Remotion lets you build videos with React. Its licence, as shipped with version 4.0.533 on 5 October, is free, commercial use included, for individuals, for-profit companies with up to 3 employees, and non-profits. Bigger companies need a company licence. Keep one idea per screen and let text move only when the line changes.

## 05 · Sound design

Freesound hosts sounds under Creative Commons licences. CC0 sounds can be used almost any way you like. Attribution sounds need a credit. Noncommercial sounds can't be used commercially, which rules out ads. A soft whoosh on scene changes and a quiet music bed go a long way.

## 06 · Captions

Transcribe your own voiceover so the captions match word for word. Hugging Face describes Qwen3 ASR as the top-ranking open-source model on its Open ASR Leaderboard. Whatever you use, fix names, brands and numbers by hand.

## 07 · Scheduling

Buffer's free plan connects up to 3 channels with 10 scheduled posts per channel. Schedule the post, then turn up in the comments yourself. Automation can publish. It can't have the conversation.

## What I'd do

Start with steps 01, 02 and 06 this week, because they save the most time. Add screen recordings next, because they make the video believable. Leave motion graphics until the script and voice feel right. And keep a human check on every fact before anything goes live.

## Sources

- FreeLLMAPI README: https://github.com/tashfeenahmed/freellmapi
- OmniRoute README: https://github.com/diegosouzapw/OmniRoute
- Kokoro-82M model card: https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M
- Hugging Face, Open TTS Leaderboard (30 Sep 2026): https://huggingface.co/blog/open-tts-leaderboard
- OBS Studio: https://obsproject.com/
- Remotion licence, v4.0.533: https://unpkg.com/remotion@4.0.533/LICENSE.md
- Freesound FAQ (licences): https://freesound.org/help/faq/
- Buffer pricing: https://buffer.com/pricing

article:
## What Anthropic announced

On 6 October Anthropic expanded **Claude Startups**, its programme for founders building companies on Claude. TechCrunch reported that it launched as part of Anthropic's SF Tech Week event. Approved startups can get:

- a free year of **Claude Team**, for up to five Premium seats, if the company is new to Team
- a one-time **$1,000 in Claude API credits**, available as soon as you're approved
- the **Claude Startup Stack**: partner discounts and credits worth up to $45,000 combined
- virtual office hours with Anthropic's Applied AI team, help building a Claude Marketplace listing, and events like Founder House and hackathons

## Who can apply

Startups founded in the last five years, or funded in the last two. You don't need venture funding: Anthropic says the programme is open to bootstrapped, pre-seed and venture-backed startups. If a VC in Anthropic's partner network backs you, you can also get up to $100K in additional API credits, claimed through your VC.

## How to apply, step by step

1. **Check the dates.** Founded in the last five years, or funded in the last two.
2. **Set up the basics.** Create a Claude Console account and use a company email that matches your website's domain.
3. **Write a short description.** Anthropic says it reviews every application, so write it like a brief: who it's for, what it does, why Claude.
4. **Apply** on the Claude Startups page.
5. **Claim Team in Console.** Once approved, you get an email linking to the Claude Startups page in Claude Console. Sign in there to claim the Team offer.
6. **Redeem partner offers** in the Console. Examples listed today: ElevenLabs (12 months free plus 33M characters), Gamma (25% off the first year of Gamma Pro annual) and Granola (3 months of Business free, up to 10 seats).

## The fine print

- Team is free only for organisations new to Team.
- The "up to $7,000" figure assumes five Premium seats at $100 per seat per month, billed annually ($6,000), plus the $1,000 credit. Fewer seats means less value.
- Credits apply to the first-party Claude API through Claude Console. They can't be used on AWS Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI or other third-party platforms.
- Partner offers come from independent companies, on their own terms, and may not combine.

## What I'd do

If I ran a small marketing-tech startup, I'd spend the $1,000 on one workflow I can measure before anything flashy. Something like scoring creator shortlists against a brief, or checking every campaign brief for missing information before it goes out. Pick a task you already do every week, so you can compare before and after.

I'd give the five Team seats to the people who write the most: briefs, reports, client emails. That's where a shared AI workspace pays back fastest.

## Sources

- Anthropic, We're expanding the Claude Startups program (6 Oct 2026): https://claude.com/blog/were-expanding-the-claude-startups-program-to-help-founders-build
- Claude for Startups programme page and FAQ: https://claude.com/programs/startups
- TechCrunch (6 Oct 2026): https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/06/anthropic-gives-startups-a-free-year-of-enterprise-service-and-1000-in-token-credits/

article:
## Three launches, one pattern

In the space of a week, three ad platforms showed tools that draft ads from what you already have.

**Google (1 October).** In an Ads Decoded post on Demand Gen and YouTube ads, Google said Asset Studio's multimodal video creation, powered by Gemini Omni, turns your website URLs and photos into high-quality videos that stakeholders can preview before you publish.

**X (6 October).** At Advertising Week New York, X launched **X Lift**. You enter your URL, X's AI generates ad options including images and copy, and it can build the whole campaign, targeting included. You set the budget. Social Media Today notes the main audience is new advertisers, and X reported that active self-serve advertisers grew 50% in Q3 2026 compared with Q3 2025.

**Meta (6 October).** Meta said advertisers can now generate video from existing static assets in Advantage+ creative, and that the feature is generally available. In Ads Creative Studio, marketers can generate video concepts and edit them to change hooks, adjust audio and clip length, add text overlays and captions, or change end scenes. Meta is also adding the ability for its business assistant to update targeting and change budgets through conversational prompts.

## Why this matters

The input is shifting. For years the creative brief was a document. Now, for a lot of small advertisers, the brief is the landing page and the assets already sitting in your folder. If the page is clear, these tools have something good to work with. If it's vague, you'll get a vague ad, just faster.

## How to test it without wasting budget

1. **Fix the page first.** Offer, price and proof near the top. That's what the AI will read.
2. **Start with what you have.** Google's own advice is that existing social assets are a solid base, as long as they follow its asset specs.
3. **Run AI drafts against your best current ad.** Same budget, same audience, one variable.
4. **Change things gradually.** Google recommends focusing on quality over quantity, so the system has time to measure.
5. **Check before anything goes live.** Every claim true, price and offer matching the page, no made-up reviews or numbers, and it still sounds like your brand.
6. **Keep a human sign-off on spend.** Especially as assistants gain the power to change budgets and targeting by prompt.

## The catch

X Lift can build the whole campaign, which means trusting X's system with targeting as well as creative. Meta's assistant is moving the same way. Automation is great at producing options. Deciding which option is true to your brand and worth the money is still your job.

## What I'd do

My rule from creator marketing carries straight over: a clear brief beats a clever tool. So I'd treat the landing page as the brief now. I'd rewrite it for one audience, one offer and one proof point, then let one of these tools draft against it, and compare the result to my best existing ad for two weeks before scaling anything.

## Sources

- Google Ads & Commerce Blog (1 Oct 2026): https://blog.google/products/ads-commerce/creating-assets-youtube-ads/
- Social Media Today on X Lift (6 Oct 2026): https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/x-launches-ai-powered-ad-creation-option/832276/
- Social Media Today on Meta at Advertising Week (6 Oct 2026): https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/meta-introduces-new-ai-powered-tools-at-advertising-week/832288/
- Common Thread Collective on Meta at Advertising Week (6 Oct 2026): https://commonthreadco.com/blogs/coachs-corner/meta-launches-generative-video-ads-and-in-conversation-checkout-at-advertising-week-ny-what-ecommerce-brands-must-do-now

title: FreeLLMAPI vs OmniRoute: two GitHub repos that stack free AI tokens, and the honest maths
hook: Two GitHub repos promise *billions* of free AI tokens.
subtitle: FreeLLMAPI says 7.4B a month. OmniRoute says ~1.62B. Here's why.

cover.concept: A laptop showing a generic code repository page, with a funnel on top merging many thin coloured pipes into one thick pipe that pours a stack of glowing token coins onto the desk. Context symbol: a generic code branch icon.
cover.label: Free tokens ↓

facts.claim: The FreeLLMAPI README headline reads: 7.4 billion tokens per month, 34 free LLM providers, 635 free model endpoints, one OpenAI-compatible endpoint (README read 7 Oct 2026).

FreeLLMAPI aggregates free tiers behind a single /v1 API; its router picks an available model, falls over to the next provider when one is rate-limited, and tracks per-key usage to stay under every free-tier cap.

FreeLLMAPI's README lists its limitations: no frontier models, variable latency, no SLA, and the endpoint's effective intelligence dips late in the day as top models hit their daily caps, then resets at UTC midnight.

FreeLLMAPI quick start: a one-line installer (Docker required), curl -fsSL https://freellmapi.co/install.sh | bash, then open http://localhost:3001 and add provider keys on the Keys page. The project is MIT-licensed.
FreeLLMAPI version 0.8.0 was published to npm on 6 Oct 2026.

The OmniRoute README headline reads: ~1.62B Free Tokens / Month. It computes the headline from free-tier pools with a published monthly budget, each shared pool counted once, and says its figures are re-audited every two weeks and move both ways.
OmniRoute install: npm i -g omniroute, the server runs on localhost:20128, and any OpenAI-compatible tool can point at http://localhost:20128/v1. OmniRoute is MIT-licensed.
OmniRoute's FREE_TIERS.md calls ~1.62B the documented recurring grant (steady) and says to use this number; ~2.22B applies to the first month only, with one-time signup credits.

OmniRoute's FREE_TIERS.md says each shared pool is counted once: Mistral's free plan is one 1B/month allowance per organisation, and listing it under five models does not make it 5B. Summed per model, its own catalogue would read ~7.4B.
OmniRoute version 3.8.51 was published to npm on 30 Sep 2026.

caption:
Two GitHub repos promise billions of free AI tokens.

I read both READMEs this week.

→ FreeLLMAPI: "7.4 billion tokens per month. 34 free LLM providers." One OpenAI-compatible endpoint that switches provider when one hits a rate limit.
→ OmniRoute: "~1.62B free tokens / month." Same idea, plus a long write-up on how they count.

Why the gap? OmniRoute counts each shared pool once. Its own docs say that adding up its catalogue model by model would read about 7.4B. But one Mistral allowance listed under five models is still one allowance.

Both numbers are the maintainers' figures, not mine.

article:
## Two repos, one promise

Free AI tokens are having a moment on GitHub. Two open-source projects keep turning up in my feed, and both make big claims at the top of their READMEs.

**FreeLLMAPI** opens with: "7.4 billion tokens per month. 34 free LLM providers. 635 free model endpoints. One OpenAI-compatible endpoint." It stacks the free tiers of many AI providers behind a single `/v1` API. A router picks an available model, falls over to the next provider when one is rate-limited, and tracks usage per key so you stay under each free cap. Version 0.8.0 landed on npm on 6 October, and the project is MIT-licensed.

**OmniRoute** headlines "~1.62B Free Tokens / Month". The core idea is the same: one local endpoint (`http://localhost:20128/v1`) that any OpenAI-compatible tool can point at, with automatic fallback when a provider says no. Version 3.8.51 shipped on npm on 30 September, also MIT.

## Why one says 7.4B and the other says 1.62B

This is the part worth reading slowly. OmniRoute's free-tier document explains that it counts each shared pool once. Its own example: Mistral's free plan is one 1B a month allowance per organisation, and listing it under five models does not make it 5B. The same document says that summing its catalogue model by model would read about 7.4B.

So OmniRoute publishes the lower, pool-deduplicated number and calls ~1.62B the documented recurring grant. A first month with one-time signup credits can reach ~2.22B, but that part does not recur.

The two headlines are not a contradiction. They are two ways of counting. Treat both as the maintainers' figures, and treat the smaller one as closer to what a single account can actually spend in a month.

## The honest catch

FreeLLMAPI's README is refreshingly direct about its limits: no frontier models, variable latency, no SLA, and the endpoint gets less capable late in the day as the best models hit their daily caps, then resets at midnight UTC. OmniRoute says its figures are re-audited every two weeks and move both ways, because providers change free tiers without much warning.

Free also has a data question. Every provider in the chain has its own terms, so check them before you send anything sensitive.

## What I'd do

- Use a router like this for drafts, research summaries, rewrites and batch jobs, where a slower or weaker model is fine.
- Keep client data, contracts and anything personal out of it.
- Start with three or four provider keys, not thirty-four. Add more once you know what you actually use.
- Keep your important workflows on a model you pay for and trust. Let free capacity take the overflow.

Getting started is short. FreeLLMAPI has a one-line installer (Docker required): `curl -fsSL https://freellmapi.co/install.sh | bash`, then open `http://localhost:3001` and add your keys on the Keys page. For OmniRoute, run `npm i -g omniroute` and point your tool at `http://localhost:20128/v1`.

My honest view: the real win isn't the giant number. It's one endpoint that keeps working when a single provider hits its limit.

article:
## What Mistral released

On 6 October Mistral launched a public preview of **Mistral Large 4**, or ML4. Its very official nickname, according to Mistral, is "le Chonk". Mistral describes it as a 1 trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model with 49 billion active parameters, and says it's the company's largest and most capable model to date.

You can try the preview API on Mistral Studio today. Mistral says it will release the weights by the end of the month. TechCrunch reported that, for now, it's only reachable through a public guardrail endpoint while safety testing finishes.

## The parts that matter for marketers

**Languages.** Mistral says a significant share of ML4's training data was multilingual, spanning more than 160 languages, including every official language of the European Union. If you run campaigns across several markets, that's the headline for you.

**Where it runs.** Mistral says ML4 was trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in its own datacentres in Europe, and that it will offer a European deployment it operates end to end under European law. For clients who ask where their data is processed, that's a real answer.

**Deliverables.** Mistral says ML4 is strong on the professional work people actually hand over: spreadsheets, slides and PDFs. On AA-Briefcase, a benchmark of long-horizon knowledge work, it reports 1,393 Elo.

## The catch

It's a preview. The open weights, which are the reason many teams care about Mistral, aren't released yet. Benchmarks in the launch post are Mistral's own claims or tests it chose to report. And "trained on 160+ languages" isn't the same as "writes great German ad copy". You still have to check.

## How to try it, step by step

1. **Pick one real brief.** Not a toy prompt. A campaign brief you've already shipped, so you know what good looks like.
2. **Ask for localised versions.** For example: "Rewrite this brief for our German and French markets. Keep every claim. Flag anything that needs a local legal or cultural check."
3. **Have a native speaker judge it.** Blind, next to your existing human version.
4. **Compare cost and speed** against the model you use today.
5. **Decide later.** If the weights land as promised, you'll have the option to run it yourself.

## What I'd do

From where I sit in Germany, multilingual work is normal, not a special project. I'd run steps 1 to 3 on one German brief this week and keep a short log of what it got right and wrong. If it holds up, a European model with open weights could be a sensible default for client work where data location matters. If not, nothing lost but an hour.

- TechCrunch (6 Oct 2026): https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/06/mistrals-new-1t-model-aims-to-leapfrog-closed-and-open-rivals/

article:
## What Anthropic released

On 28 September Anthropic released **Claude Sonnet 5.5**, the second model in the Claude 5.5 family after Opus 5.5. Anthropic says it generates output 30%+ faster than Sonnet 5 and costs up to 30% less per task in its testing, at the same per-token price: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.

## The part marketers should notice

Anthropic describes Sonnet 5.5 as strongest at well-scoped everyday tasks and at "creating polished documents, slides, and spreadsheets". Early testers said it can follow slide templates to create decks that need minimal editing.

The most concrete example is Anthropic's own: it gave the model a public company's quarterly earnings materials, call transcripts and a slide template, and asked for a 10-slide operating review. Two experts judged the first draft ready to send as is.

That's an internal test, not an independent benchmark, so treat it as a promise to check, not a result to quote to your boss. Still, it's a clear signal that "build me a deck from my template" is becoming a normal workflow.

## The 4-step workflow

**01 · Pick Sonnet 5.5.** Anthropic says it's available on all platforms. In the Claude apps the default effort is Medium, which is fine for a first draft.

**02 · Upload two things.** Your real slide template, and your source material: the brief, the report, the data export. The template is what stops it inventing a layout.

**03 · Prompt with rules.** Something like:

> Use my template. 10 slides, one message per slide. Cite the source for every number. Flag anything you guessed.

**04 · Check every number.** Open the sources, compare, correct. The model drafts. You sign it off.

## When to use Opus instead

Anthropic's developer guide is direct about this: Sonnet 5.5 fits best when the task has a clear spec and a way to check the result, and for the hardest long-horizon work an Opus model is the better choice. A deck built from clear inputs suits Sonnet. A strategy that needs judgement across messy, conflicting inputs may be better on Opus 5.5.

## What I'd do

I'd start with the deck I build most often, like a monthly campaign review, and run Sonnet 5.5 alongside my usual process for one cycle. I'd track two things: time to a first draft, and how many corrections I make before it's sendable. If the corrections stay high, I'd look at my inputs first. A vague brief makes a vague deck, whichever model you use.

And I'd never let a number go out that I haven't traced back to its source.

- Anthropic developer guide, Building with Claude Sonnet 5.5 (28 Sep 2026): https://claude.dev/blog/building-with-claude-sonnet-5-5/
